bibliographic.title: Rethinking LLMOps for Fraud and AML: Building a Compliance-Grade LLM Serving Stack
bibliographic.authors: Prathamesh Vasudeo Naik; Naresh Dintakurthi; Yue Wang
bibliographic.citation_apa: Naik, P. V., Dintakurthi, N., & Wang, Y. (2026). Rethinking LLMOps for fraud and AML: Building a compliance-grade LLM serving stack. arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.11232.

methodology.method_family: systems engineering with controlled serving benchmarks and synthetic workload evaluation
methodology.study_design: technical architecture proposal with reproducibility track and controlled serving benchmarks on public synthetic AML datasets
methodology.sample_description: Public synthetic AML datasets (IBM AML, SAML-D) converted into prefix-heavy compliance prompts; controlled serving benchmarks; no proprietary customer records or institution-specific data
methodology.technology_context: Self-hosted open-weight models (Meta Llama, Alibaba Qwen); vLLM-style runtime; PagedAttention; Automatic Prefix Caching; multi-adapter serving; LLM-as-judge evaluation framework with deterministic compliance checks

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper directly addresses LLM deployment in regulated financial AML/fraud contexts and explicitly discusses auditability, operational control, governance, and output-quality validation within a compliance-grade serving stack. Its primary contribution is workload-aware LLMOps and serving optimization rather than conversational governance, human oversight, contestation, or chatbot/agent interaction design; it is therefore better classified as supporting evidence for operational-technical governance in regulated LLM systems than as central conversational-governance evidence.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter text was provided; full-text verification is needed to confirm whether later sections add conversational oversight, handoff, logging, or governance mechanisms beyond serving infrastructure.

appraisal.notes: Objectives and methods are clearly aligned for serving-stack performance claims. Authors transparently scope findings to public synthetic data and serving benchmarks, limiting transferability to proprietary institutional AML workflows and to conversational-governance claims not evidenced in the excerpt.

cerqual.explanation: The study is internally coherent and reports concrete benchmark metrics, but evidence is based on synthetic public datasets and serving benchmarks rather than live regulated conversational systems; relevance to conversational governance is partial and mainly indirect through compliance deployment concerns.

coding.theme: Compliance-grade LLM serving infrastructure in regulated financial workloads
coding.subtheme: Workload-aware LLMOps for fraud and AML

synthesis.main_claim: Fraud and AML compliance LLM workloads are prefix-dominated and require a workload-aware, self-hosted LLMOps serving stack with caching, multi-adapter orchestration, and LLM-as-judge quality gates to meet regulated deployment needs for latency, auditability, and output validity.
synthesis.contribution: Maps concrete serving optimizations to AML/fraud workloads and reports large throughput and latency gains on public synthetic benchmarks while proposing a reproducibility track and pre-production evaluation framework for compliance-grade rollout decisions.
synthesis.limitations: Evidence is limited to public synthetic AML datasets and controlled serving benchmarks; authors state results should not be interpreted as disclosure of proprietary financial-institution systems; conversational governance mechanisms are not the paper's main focus in the provided text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on operational-technical governance, compliance validation, and regulated deployment constraints for LLMs in financial AML/fraud contexts; do not treat as primary evidence on conversational governance, human contestation, or chatbot interaction design.

evidence.claim: Paper targets regulated financial AML/fraud use of LLMs.

evidence.claim: Compliance workloads differ from open-ended conversational chat.

evidence.claim: Governance is integrated into the controlled deployment stack.
evidence.excerpt: the ability to integrate model selection, serving optimization, governance, and quality validation within a controlled deployment stack

evidence.claim: Auditability and operational control are stated deployment requirements.
evidence.excerpt: output validity, auditability, and operational control are equally important

evidence.claim: LLM-as-judge framework includes deterministic compliance checks and expert calibration.

evidence.claim: Reported serving benchmark improvements on synthetic AML workloads.
evidence.excerpt: workload-aware tuning improved throughput from 612–650 to 3,600 requests/hour, reduced P99 latency from 31–38 seconds to 6.4–8.7 seconds

evidence.claim: Authors limit generalizability to synthetic serving evidence.
evidence.excerpt: These results should be interpreted as serving-stack and workload-shape evidence on public synthetic data

evidence.excerpt: MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, and G-Eval show that strong judges can align with human preferences
